Zoar
ZOH-ar
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Tsoar, "little"; the small city of the plain to which Lot fled and which was spared at his request.

📖 Biblical Definition

Zoar was one of the cities of the plain near the Salt Sea, originally called Bela, the small town to which Lot fled when God rained fire and brimstone upon Sodom and Gomorrah. As the angels urged Lot to escape to the mountain, he begged instead to flee to a nearby little city: "Behold now, this city is near to flee unto, and it is a little one... is it not a little one? and my soul shall live" (Gen 19:20). The LORD granted his plea: "I have accepted thee concerning this thing also, that I will not overthrow this city... Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar" (Gen 19:21-22) — "little." Indeed, the angel said he could do nothing until Lot had come there; the rescue of one righteous man held back the judgment until he was safe. Yet Lot, who had begged for Zoar, soon feared to dwell there and went up into the mountain to live in a cave (Gen 19:30). Zoar stands in the dictionary as the little city of refuge spared for Lot's sake, a witness to the mercy of God who hears the prayers of the weak and delivers the righteous from judgment, and a sober picture of Lot himself, whose worldly choices had so impoverished his faith that he scarcely knew where to find rest even in the mercy God granted him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The small city of the plain ("little") to which Lot fled from Sodom and which God spared at his plea (Gen 19:20-22); a witness to God's mercy in delivering the righteous from judgment.

ZOAR, proper noun. "Little"; a small city of the plain, originally called Bela.

Where Lot fled when God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.

Spared at Lot's plea: "is it not a little one? and my soul shall live" (Gen 19:20).

The angel could do nothing until Lot had come there (Gen 19:22).

Soon left by Lot, who feared and went up to a cave in the mountain (Gen 19:30).

📖 Key Scripture

Gen 19:20 — "Behold now, this city is near to flee unto, and it is a little one: Oh, let me escape thither, (is it not a little one?) and my soul shall live."

Gen 19:22 — "Haste thee, escape thither; for I cannot do any thing till thou be come thither. Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar."

2 Pet 2:7 — "And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked:"

2 Pet 2:9 — "The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Zoar needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are God's mercy in delivering the righteous before judgment falls, and the impoverished faith of Lot, whose worldly choices left him weak even in his rescue.

expand to see more

Mercy-doubted correction. Some imagine God deaf to the prayers of the weak and faltering. Lot, frightened and faltering, begged for the little city, and God granted it, even holding back the fire until His servant was safe. The dictionary holds that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation (2 Pet 2:9); He hears the trembling prayers of weak believers, and the rescue of even one righteous man may stay the falling of judgment until he is safe.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the impoverishing cost of worldly choices. Lot, who had once pitched his tent toward Sodom for its good land, was so weakened by his worldliness that he could scarcely find rest even in the mercy God granted, begging for Zoar and then fearing to stay there. The dictionary commends the warning: the believer who makes his home among the wicked for worldly gain may be saved, yet so as by fire, his faith impoverished and his life barren, a righteous man with little to show for his years.
